राजस्थान में बदला मौसम, सुबह-शाम ठंड और दिन में तेज धूप
जयपुर। राजस्थान में मौसम का मिजाज बदलने लगा है। सुबह और रात के समय हल्की सर्दी का असर बढ़ रहा है, जबकि दिन में तेज धूप के कारण तापमान में बढ़ोतरी हो रही है।
मंगलवार सुबह श्रीगंगानगर सहित प्रदेश के कई जिलों में हल्का कोहरा छाया रहा। इससे कुछ स्थानों पर दृश्यता प्रभावित हुई। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार प्रदेश में आगामी एक सप्ताह मौसम शुष्क रहने की संभावना है।
बंगाल की खाड़ी में सक्रिय चक्रवाती तूफान मुरासु का राजस्थान के मौसम पर कोई विशेष प्रभाव पड़ने की संभावना नहीं है। पिछले 24 घंटों के दौरान प्रदेश के अधिकांश हिस्सों में आसमान साफ रहा और दिनभर धूप खिली रही।
सोमवार को बाड़मेर, जैसलमेर, जोधपुर, सीकर, अलवर और जयपुर सहित कई शहरों के अधिकतम तापमान में एक से दो डिग्री सेल्सियस तक बढ़ोतरी दर्ज की गई। वहीं, रात के तापमान में गिरावट से सुबह और देर रात सर्दी का अहसास बढ़ने लगा है।
सोमवार को फतेहपुर में न्यूनतम तापमान 13.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया, जो प्रदेश में सबसे कम रहा। दिन और रात के तापमान में अंतर के कारण मौसम में दोहरा मिजाज देखने को मिल रहा है।
दिन में धूप से गर्माहट बनी हुई है, जबकि सुबह और शाम हल्की ठंड महसूस की जा रही है। मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र जयपुर के अनुसार प्रदेश में आगामी एक सप्ताह तक मौसम साफ और शुष्क रहने की संभावना है।
इस दौरान बारिश के आसार नहीं हैं। दिन में तेज धूप के कारण कुछ शहरों में अधिकतम तापमान में मामूली बढ़ोतरी हो सकती है, जबकि रात के तापमान में गिरावट से हल्की सर्दी का दौर बना रहेगा।

प्रयागराज में मौसम तेजी से ठंड की ओर अग्रसर है। सूर्य की किरणों में भी गर्मी अब नहीं है। मौसम ...और पढ़ें

जागरण संवाददाता, प्रयागराज। नवंबर की शुरुआत के साथ ही मौसम ने करवट लेनी शुरू कर दी है। दिन में धूप तो निकल रही है, लेकिन अब उसकी तपिश में पहले जैसी तेजी नहीं रही। दोपहर की धूप में न उमस है और न ही गर्मी का वह अहसास। दूसरी ओर रात का तापमान धीरे-धीरे नीचे उतरने लगा है।
मौसम के बदलने के संकेत
मौसम के बदलते मिजाज के संकेत मिलने लगे हैं। यानी अब सर्दी दरवाजे पर खड़ी है। मौसम विभाग का अनुमान है कि नवंबर के दूसरे सप्ताह से ठंड का असर और बढ़ेगा। दिन का तापमान 28 डिग्री से नीचे पहुंच जाएगा, जबकि रात का पारा 18 डिग्री तक लुढ़क सकता है।
रात में सर्दी की आहट
सोमवार को शहर का अधिकतम तापमान 31.8 डिग्री सेल्सियस और न्यूनतम तापमान 21.2 डिग्री दर्ज किया गया। खास बात यह है कि न्यूनतम तापमान अभी भी सामान्य से 4.4 डिग्री अधिक बना हुआ है। इसके बावजूद रात के तापमान में गिरावट का रुख सर्दी की आहट दे रहा है।
चार नवंबर की सुबह कोहरा छाएगा
पिछले 24 घंटे में बारिश नहीं हुई। सुबह वातावरण में नमी 91 प्रतिशत रही, जो शाम तक घटकर 75 प्रतिशत पर पहुंच गई। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार चार नवंबर की सुबह हल्का कोहरा छा सकता है। हालांकि दिन चढ़ने के साथ आसमान साफ होगा और धूप निकलेगी। इन दोनों दिनों में अधिकतम तापमान 30 और न्यूनतम 20 डिग्री के आसपास रहने की संभावना है।
आठ नवंबर तक दिन में भी महसूस होगी ठंड
तापमान में गिरावट का सिलसिला पांच नवंबर से ज्यादा स्पष्ट दिखाई देने लगेगा। इस दिन न्यूनतम तापमान 18 डिग्री तक पहुंचने का अनुमान है। छह और सात नवंबर को भी रात का तापमान इसी स्तर पर बना रह सकता है। वहीं अधिकतम तापमान 29 डिग्री रहने की संभावना है। आठ नवंबर तक दिन का पारा भी गिरकर 28 डिग्री तक पहुंच सकता है। यानी अभी दोपहर में धूप के सहारे गर्मी का एहसास भले बना हुआ है, लेकिन आने वाले दिनों में सुबह और देर रात हल्की ठंड लोगों को गर्म कपड़ों की याद दिलाने लगेगी।

जागरण संवाददाता, पटना। पछुआ के प्रभाव से प्रदेश का मौसम फिलहाल शुष्क और सामान्य बना रहेगा। सुबह और रात में हल्की ठंड का अहसास होगा, जबकि दो दिनों के दौरान धुंध में वृद्धि के आसार हैं।
मौसम साफ रहने और पछुआ हवा के असर से दिन में धूप की तल्खी बढ़ने की संभावना है। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, अगले 24 घंटे के दौरान अधिकतम तापमान में एक से तीन डिग्री सेल्सियस तक वृद्धि की संभावना है।
सोमवार को पटना सहित 18 जिलों के तापमान में वृद्धि दर्ज की गई। पटना के अधिकतम तापमान में तीन डिग्री वृद्धि के साथ 29.9 डिग्री सेल्सियस व 33.9 डिग्री सेल्सियस के साथ औरंगबाद में सर्वाधिक तापमान दर्ज किया गया।
बीते 24 घंटे के दौरान नवादा के रजौली में 3.6 मिमी एवं नवादा के मेसकौर में 2.8 मिमी वर्षा दर्ज की गई। बीते 24 घंटे के दौरान अनेक स्थानों के अधिकतम तापमान में दो से तीन डिग्री सेल्सियस की वृद्धि दर्ज की गई।
प्रदेश में मौसम के बदलते तेवर के कारण दिन और रात के तापमान में अंतर होने से हल्की ठंड और दोपहर में गर्मी का एहसास हो सकता है। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार माह में प्रदेश का अधिकतम तापमान सामान्य से अधिक रहने के कारण विशेष ठंड का प्रभाव नहीं होगा।

चक्रवाती तूफान अर्णब के बाद काशी में मौसम सामान्य हो रहा।
सुबह धुंध छाई रही, दिन में धूप से तापमान बढ़ा।
आगामी दिनों में रातें ठंडी होंगी, सुबह कोहरा रहेगा।
जागरण संवाददाता, वाराणसी। चक्रवाती तूफान अर्णब का असर कमजोर पड़ने के साथ ही काशी में मौसम धीरे-धीरे सामान्य होने लगा है। हालांकि, सोमवार की सुबह धुंध में नहाई रही। इसके चलते दृश्यता घटकर 200 मीटर तक पहुंच गई। दिन चढ़ने के साथ धुंध छंटी और धूप निकलने से अधिकतम तापमान सामान्य के करीब पहुंच गया।
सोमवार को अधिकतम तापमान 31.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया, जो सामान्य से महज 0.1 डिग्री कम रहा। वहीं न्यूनतम तापमान 20 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा, जो सामान्य से तीन डिग्री अधिक है। इस दौरान आर्द्रता 78 से 96 प्रतिशत के बीच बनी रही। हालांकि मंगलवार को मौसम का रुख दूसरा ही रहा और कोहारा सिर्फ अंचलों में रहा और शहर में धूप भी चटख रही।
बीते दिनों अर्णब के प्रभाव से हुई वर्षा के कारण तापमान में उल्लेखनीय गिरावट आई थी। शुक्रवार को अधिकतम तापमान सामान्य से 9.1 डिग्री नीचे 22.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच गया था। इसके बाद मौसम साफ होने और धूप निकलने से इसमें लगातार वृद्धि हुई। रविवार को अधिकतम तापमान 30.2 डिग्री और सोमवार को 31.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया।
दिन में बढ़ेगी गर्मी, रात में गिरेगा पारा
मौसम विज्ञानी डा. अतुल कुमार सिंह के अनुसार दिन के अधिकतम तापमान में प्रभावी वृद्धि होगी और यह सामान्य के करीब पहुंच जाएगा। इसके बाद आगामी दो-तीन दिनों में न्यूनतम तापमान में दो से तीन डिग्री सेल्सियस की गिरावट आने की संभावना है। सुबह के समय कहीं-कहीं हल्के से मध्यम कोहरे की स्थिति बन सकती है, जो दिन चढ़ने के साथ जल्दी छंट जाएगा। ऐसे में दिन में गर्माहट बढ़ेगी, जबकि सुबह और रात में अपेक्षाकृत ठंड का एहसास होगा।

Delhi Weather Update: दिल्ली में मौसम का मिजाज बदलने लगा है और सुबह-शाम हल्की ठंड महसूस होने लगी है. दिन में धूप निकलने से फिलहाल राहत बनी हुई है. मौसम विभाग ने 4 नवंबर से लेकर अगले 5 से 7 दिनों तक का पूर्वानुमान जारी किया है. जानिए राजधानी में तापमान कितना रहेगा और बारिश को लेकर क्या अपडेट है.

राष्ट्रीय राजधानी दिल्ली में मौसम का मिजाज धीरे-धीरे बदलने लगा है. सुबह और शाम के समय हल्की ठंड महसूस होने लगी है, जबकि दिन में धूप निकलने से लोगों को राहत मिल रही है. तापमान में गिरावट के साथ अब मौसम में ठंडक बढ़ने के संकेत मिलने लगे हैं. इस बीच मौसम विभाग ने अपना दैनिक बुलेटिन जारी किया है. इसके अनुसार 4 नवंबर को दिल्ली में आसमान साफ रहने के साथ सुबह हल्की धुंध छा सकती है. वहीं, अगले कुछ दिनों तक बारिश की संभावना नहीं है.
दिल्ली में 4 नवंबर को कैसा रहेगा मौसम?
मौसम विभाग के पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार, 4 नवंबर 2026 को दिल्ली में आसमान मुख्य रूप से साफ रहने की संभावना है. हालांकि, सुबह के समय हल्की धुंध या कोहरा देखने को मिल सकता है. इस दौरान दिन का अधिकतम तापमान 27 से 29 डिग्री सेल्सियस और न्यूनतम तापमान 14 से 16 डिग्री सेल्सियस के आसपास रहने का अनुमान है. दिन में हल्की धूप खिलने से मौसम सुहाना बना रहेगा. वहीं, सुबह और शाम के समय ठंड का अहसास ज्यादा हो सकता है. खबर लिखे जानें मौसम विभाग के अनुसार 4 नवंबर को दिल्ली के किसी भी जिले के लिए कोई गंभीर चेतावनी जारी नहीं की गई है.
अगले 5 से 7 दिनों तक कैसा रहेगा दिल्ली का मौसम?
मौसम विभाग के मुताबिक, दिल्ली में अगले 5 से 7 दिनों तक मौसम शुष्क और आसमान साफ रहने का अनुमान है. इस दौरान बारिश की कोई संभावना नहीं जताई गई है. 5 से 9 नवंबर के बीच अधिकतम तापमान 27 से 30 डिग्री सेल्सियस और न्यूनतम तापमान 13 से 17 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रह सकता है. हालांकि, सुबह के समय धुंध का असर बना रह सकता है. तापमान में गिरावट के साथ आने वाले दिनों में ठंड का अहसास और बढ़ने की संभावना है.

Science News: क्या आपने कभी गौर किया है कि पिछले कुछ सालों में गर्मियों का प्रकोप पहले से कहीं ज्यादा बेकाबू और मौसम का मिजाज अजीब क्यों हो गया है? हम अक्सर सुनते हैं कि "तापमान बढ़ रहा है", लेकिन अब विज्ञान ने एक ऐसा कड़वा सच उजागर किया है जो इससे कहीं ज्यादा खतरनाक है, धरती न केवल गर्म हो रही है, बल्कि उसके गर्म होने की रफ्तार भी अब दोगुनी गति से तेज हो चुकी है। जर्मनी के प्रतिष्ठित पोट्सडैम इंस्टीट्यूट फॉर क्लाइमेट इंपैक्ट रिसर्च (PIK) द्वारा किए गए एक ऐतिहासिक अध्ययन में पहली बार सांख्यिकीय रूप से यह साबित हुआ है कि 2015 के आसपास से ग्लोबल वार्मिंग की रफ्तार में एक बड़ा और अभूतपूर्व उछाल आया है। आधुनिक तापमान रिकॉर्ड की शुरुआत यानी 1880 के बाद से पृथ्वी कभी भी इतनी तेजी से नहीं तपी, जितनी तेजी से वह पिछले एक दशक में गर्म हुई है। वैज्ञानिक पत्रिका जिओफिजिकल रिसर्च लेटर्स (Geophysical Research Letters) में प्रकाशित इस शोध ने पूरी दुनिया के पर्यावरणविदों और नीति निर्माताओं की नींद उड़ा दी है।
जब 'वार्मिंग स्पीड' हुई लगभग दोगुनी
अध्ययन के अनुसार, 2015 के बाद यानी करीब पिछले 10 सालों में पृथ्वी का तापमान लगभग 0.35°C प्रति दशक की खतरनाक दर से बढ़ा है।1970 से 2015 के बीच पृथ्वी का औसत तापमान लगभग 0.2°C प्रति दशक से कम की दर से बढ़ रहा था। इसका सीधा मतलब ये है कि पिछले एक दशक में ग्लोबल वार्मिंग की स्पीड लगभग दो गुनी हो चुकी है।
पिछले 10 सालों में तापमान दर हुई खतरनाक
वैज्ञानिकों ने प्राकृतिक 'शोर' को हटाकर कैसे खोजा यह सच?
ग्लोबल वार्मिंग की असली गति को समझना इतना आसान नहीं होता, क्योंकि प्रकृति समय-समय पर अपने तरीके से तापमान को ऊपर या नीचे करती रहती है।
- अल नीनो: प्रशांत महासागर की यह प्राकृतिक घटना वायुमंडल में गर्मी छोड़कर पृथ्वी को अस्थायी रूप से अधिक गर्म कर देती है।
- ज्वालामुखी विस्फोट: ज्वालामुखी से निकलने वाले कण सूरज की रोशनी को अंतरिक्ष में वापस परावर्तित कर देते हैं, जिससे अस्थायी ठंडक आती है।
- सौर चक्र (Solar Maximum): सूर्य की 11-वर्षीय सक्रियता का चक्र भी पृथ्वी तक पहुंचने वाली ऊर्जा में थोड़ा उतार-चढ़ाव लाता है।
क्या 2023 और 2024 के रिकॉर्ड तापमान ने आंकड़े बिगाड़े?
अध्ययन में एक बड़ा सवाल यह था कि क्या 2023 और 2024 में दर्ज किए गए रिकॉर्ड-तोड़ तापमान की वजह से यह ट्रेंड ज्यादा खतरनाक दिख रहा है? शोधकर्ताओं ने अल नीनो और सोलर मैक्सिमम के प्रभावों को घटाकर जब डेटा को दोबारा जांचा, तो 2023 और 2024 के तापमान आंकड़े थोड़े कम जरूर हुए, लेकिन वे फिर भी मानव इतिहास के सबसे गर्म साल ही बने रहे। इसके अलावा, वार्मिंग की गति तेज होने के संकेत 2013-2014 से ही सभी 5 प्रमुख डेटासेट्स में दिखाई देने लगे थे।
'1.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस' की सीमा टूटने का खतरा
पेरिस समझौते की 1.5°C की डेडलाइन
साल 2015 में हुए पेरिस जलवायु समझौते के तहत दुनिया के तमाम देशों ने मिलकर यह संकल्प लिया था कि वे वैश्विक तापमान में बढ़ोतरी को औद्योगिक क्रांति से पहले के स्तर से 1.5°C से अधिक नहीं होने देंगे। लेकिन इस नए अध्ययन ने चेतावनी की घंटी बजा दी है। मुख्य अध्ययनकर्ता प्रोफेसर स्टीफन राह्मस्टॉर्फ कहते हैं कि "यदि पिछले 10 वर्षों में मापी गई तापमान बढ़ोतरी की यही रफ्तार जारी रहती है, तो 2030 से पहले ही हम पेरिस समझौते की 1.5°C की सीमा को स्थायी रूप से पार कर जाएंगे। पृथ्वी कितनी तेजी से आगे गर्म होगी, यह इस बात पर निर्भर करता है कि हम जीवाश्म ईंधनों से CO2 उत्सर्जन को कितनी जल्दी शून्य पर लाते हैं।"
भविष्य के लिए चेतावनी
यह अध्ययन हमें साफ-साफ चेतावनी देता है कि जलवायु परिवर्तन का संकट अब सिर्फ 'भविष्य की बात' नहीं रहा, बल्कि यह हमारे दरवाजे पर एक बहुत तेज गति से दस्तक दे रहा है। समय हाथ से फिसल रहा है, और यदि वैश्विक स्तर पर कोयला, तेल और गैस जैसे जीवाश्म ईंधनों के इस्तेमाल पर तुरंत रोक नहीं लगाई गई, तो आने वाले दशक में मौसम के ऐसे जानलेवा मिजाज देखने को मिल सकते हैं, जिनकी कल्पना भी नहीं की गई है।

जोधपुर में सर्दी बढ़ने की संभावना, अक्टूबर में तापमान औसत से ऊपर रहा
जोधपुर में न्यूनतम तापमान 20 डिग्री से नीचे आ गया है और रात में सर्दी बढ़ रही है। अक्टूबर में अधिकतम तापमान का औसत 36.1 डिग्री रहा जो पिछले साल से अधिक था। मौसम विभाग ने नवंबर में ठंड बढ़ने और आने वाले दिनों में तापमान में उतार-चढ़ाव की संभावना जताई है।
रात में ठंड बढ़ी, नवंबर में सर्दी बढ़ने की संभावना; जानिए अक्टूबर में कैसा रहा मौसम जोधपुर में मौसम में उतार-चढ़ाव का दौर जारी है। न्यूनतम तापमान 20 डिग्री से नीचे आ गया है। वहीं, अधिकतम तापमान में थोड़ा उतार-चढ़ाव बना हुआ है। पिछले कुछ दिनों से अधिकतम तापमान 32-33 डिग्री बना हुआ है। तापमान में गिरावट नवंबर में सर्दी के बढ़ने की संभावना है। मंगलवार को अधिकतम तापमान 34.

Extreme heat may raise suicide risk by disrupting sleep, emotional control: Study
A World Bank and Georgetown University study links extreme heat to higher suicide risk, highlighting the lesser-known effects of climate change on the mental health of millions.
Extreme heat, becoming increasingly common in India and around the world, could do more than take a physical toll on the human body.
Climate-induced heat could also affect mental health, increasing suicide risk by disrupting sleep and making it harder to manage emotions, a new study by the World Bank and Georgetown University has found.
Published in Environmental Research, the study examined how rising temperatures are potentially associated with suicide risk in Bangladesh, a country particularly vulnerable to climate change.
The researchers stressed that the findings point to possible pathways linking heat and suicide risk, rather than establishing that high temperatures directly cause suicide.
Researchers found that the risk began to rise at temperatures of 28°C and was highest at 35°C.
The findings provide another look into how climate change could affect mental well-being, particularly in countries where millions face prolonged exposure to extreme heat and have limited access to cooling.
“Extreme heat events are becoming more frequent, longer, and more intense due to climate change,” said lead author Syed Shabab Wahid, an assistant professor at Georgetown University and a World Bank researcher.
HOW HEAT AFFECTS SLEEP AND EMOTIONS
The study followed 7,492 people across two rounds of a nationally representative survey in Bangladesh. Researchers examined suicide risk alongside exposure to high temperatures, sleep quality and the ability to regulate emotions.
At 35°C, poor sleep accounted for 29.5% of the observed association between heat exposure and suicide risk. Difficulties in regulating emotions accounted for another 1.8%.
Wahid explained that “high ambient temperatures can impair restorative sleep patterns.”
Heat can also weaken a person's ability to manage difficult emotions and cope with psychological distress.
Sleep is essential for the brain and body to recover. But as India experienced this year, warmer nights are making it increasingly difficult to get adequate rest. When nights remain hot, people may struggle to sleep well, leaving them tired and less equipped to deal with everyday stress.
“Without identifying how ambient heat disrupts daily physiological functions and emotional control,” Wahid said, public health officials and clinicians face limitations in developing targeted interventions.
RISING TEMPERATURES, RISING MENTAL HEALTH RISKS
The association between extreme heat and suicide risk was stronger during summer and among poorer and less educated populations, highlighting how social and economic conditions can influence vulnerability.
Wahid said the research could help health agencies “monitor heat waves alongside sleep quality disruption indicators” to identify when preventive support may be needed.
He also called for “sleep preservation, household cooling access, and community-based emotional regulation training” as potential interventions during heatwaves.
Looking ahead, researchers want to explore affordable cooling solutions, better-designed homes and ways to protect people from heat during the night.
“This line of research can integrate mental healthcare into national climate resilience planning and early warning systems,” Wahid said.

A new assessment of the April 2024 heatwave shows that climate change is no longer only an infrastructure, water or livelihood crisis. It is also entering the most private spaces of urban life: pregnancy, childbirth and newborn care. Across India, Bangladesh and the Philippines, the heat during that month was associated with an estimated 16,150 additional premature births, including 10,600 linked specifically to human-caused global warming. India accounted for 8,830 of those climate-linked cases, according to a study by Zero Carbon Analytics cited in the report.
The finding matters because it shifts the climate-health discussion from broad exposure to a specific pressure on health systems. Heatwaves are generally measured through temperature records, excess deaths, electricity demand or water stress. The study instead connects an extreme heat event to premature births, a health outcome that can impose long-term costs on families, hospitals and public services. It also shows why heat action plans cannot be treated only as emergency arrangements for outdoor workers, older people or people with existing illnesses.
The April 2024 event was unusual in both scale and attribution. Across the three countries, premature births were estimated to be 3.6 per cent higher in India, 11.9 per cent higher in Bangladesh and 10 per cent higher in the Philippines than during a normal April. The report distinguishes between all additional premature births during the heat and the smaller number attributed specifically to human-caused warming. In India, the latter figure was estimated at 8,830; Bangladesh accounted for 1,479 and the Philippines for 263.
That distinction is important for interpreting the evidence. The 16,150 figure describes the estimated increase during an unusually hot month compared with a normal April. The 10,600 figure describes the estimated portion that would not have occurred in a world without human-caused temperature rise. The numbers are therefore not interchangeable, but together they indicate how climate change can amplify an existing health risk.
The study also found that the heat event in South Asia became approximately 45 times more likely because of human-caused climate change. In the Philippines, researchers assessed that a comparable event would have been almost impossible without that influence. These findings do not mean that every premature birth during the month was caused by heat or climate change. They indicate a population-level association between the intensity of the heat event and an increase in premature births, with a defined share attributed to human-driven warming.
The geography of the burden is equally significant for India. Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Jharkhand were estimated to account for approximately two-thirds of the country’s additional premature births during the event. These states combine large populations with substantial demand for maternal and newborn health services. The concentration means that a national climate-health response cannot rely only on broad advisories issued from central or state capitals. It must reach pregnant women, frontline health workers, primary health centres, maternity hospitals and local administrations in the districts where exposure and service pressure overlap.
The report does not provide a complete district-level assessment of hospital capacity, access to cooling or the socio-economic profile of affected mothers. That limits what can be concluded about the precise pathways from heat exposure to premature birth. However, the distribution of estimated cases identifies where more detailed surveillance is needed. It also underlines the importance of connecting climate information with routine maternal health data rather than treating the two systems as separate administrative concerns.
The medical risk associated with premature birth extends beyond delivery. Premature babies face a higher likelihood of serious health problems in the early stages of life, and the report notes possible effects on physical growth, brain and nervous-system development, and later social and economic outcomes. For families, this can mean longer hospital stays, higher care requirements and prolonged uncertainty. For the public health system, it can mean additional demand for neonatal care, trained staff, equipment and follow-up services.
Dr Rashmi Agrawalla, associate professor in Community and Family Medicine and climate-change nodal officer at AIIMS Guwahati, said pregnant women in climate-vulnerable countries such as India are directly exposed to these risks. She identified anaemia, poor nutrition and prolonged outdoor work as factors that can intensify heat-related risks during pregnancy. Her comments point to an important institutional issue: exposure is not determined by temperature alone. It is shaped by housing conditions, work, nutrition, access to water, the ability to rest and the distance to medical care.
This is where the urban dimension becomes visible even when the most affected locations are not limited to large metropolitan areas. Heat is experienced through homes, workplaces, roads, public transport, hospitals and neighbourhood services. Pregnant women living in dense settlements or poorly ventilated housing may have limited access to indoor cooling. Those working outdoors or in informal employment may not be able to change their hours or stop work during the hottest part of the day. A heat warning has limited value if people cannot act on it without losing income, care access or mobility.
The study’s projections for 2050 make the issue more consequential. Using two climate scenarios, it estimated that India could experience more than 15,000 additional premature births during a normal April by the middle of the century. In this projection, a normal April around 2050 could carry a greater premature-birth burden than the exceptionally hot April of 2024. Uttar Pradesh was projected to face the largest impact, followed by Bihar and Rajasthan. For Bangladesh, the report estimated approximately 1,500 additional premature births during a normal April by mid-century, with the Dhaka division most affected, followed by Chattogram and Rajshahi.
These projections should be read as estimates under specified temperature scenarios, not as a fixed forecast. Their policy value lies in showing how an extreme event can become part of ordinary seasonal conditions as the baseline temperature rises. The central planning challenge is therefore not only how to respond to exceptional heat, but how to redesign routine maternal and neonatal services for a hotter climate.
The report says that existing maternal-health policies and heat-action plans in India, Bangladesh and the Philippines do not yet systematically include protections for pregnant women and newborns. That gap concerns both policy design and implementation. Health advisories for pregnant women, access to cooling, early-warning systems and heat-sensitive antenatal care would need to be integrated into local service delivery. Hospitals and primary health facilities would also need protocols for identifying heat stress and maintaining safe conditions during prolonged hot periods.
Such integration requires coordination between departments that often work on separate timelines. Meteorological agencies issue forecasts and warnings; health departments manage antenatal and neonatal services; municipal bodies influence water supply, public spaces, housing conditions and local cooling facilities; labour authorities address workplace exposure; and community health workers maintain contact with households. Without a clear institutional chain linking a heat alert to specific action for pregnant women, the warning may remain informational rather than protective.
Dr Joanne Bentley-McCune, the study’s lead author and a senior research analyst at Zero Carbon Analytics, said rising temperatures were making extreme heat events more frequent and intense and increasing the risk of premature birth. She pointed to improved antenatal care, access to cooling and timely warning systems as measures that could reduce some risks, while also stating that these actions cannot eliminate the full burden created by climate change. The report therefore places adaptation and emissions reduction in the same frame: health systems must prepare for heat already occurring, while governments also limit the warming that increases future exposure.
The wider international response is beginning to recognise this connection. The report refers to a global framework launched by the World Health Organization, the World Meteorological Organization, UNICEF and the United Nations Population Fund to track extreme-heat risks for pregnant women, newborns and children. It also notes that health is expected to receive attention at the upcoming COP31 climate conference and that the United Nations climate leadership has called for action on heat-related impacts during pregnancy and childbirth.
For Indian cities and states, the immediate evidence is not a case for attributing every adverse birth outcome to climate change. It is a case for improving the way risk is recorded and managed. Maternal-health data, heat exposure, occupational conditions, nutrition and access to cooling need to be considered together if authorities are to identify vulnerable groups and allocate services effectively. The estimated concentration of cases in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and Jharkhand provides a starting point for that work, but the supplied study does not establish how the burden varies between urban and rural areas or between different income groups.
What the evidence confirms is narrower but important: the April 2024 heat event coincided with a measurable increase in estimated premature births across three Asian countries, and a substantial share of that increase was attributed to human-caused warming. What remains to be established through further surveillance is how heat exposure operates across different communities and which interventions reduce the risk most effectively. The developments to monitor are the incorporation of pregnancy and newborn protections into heat-action plans, the availability of local cooling and warning systems, and whether maternal-health programmes begin treating extreme heat as a routine climate-related risk rather than an occasional emergency.

HEALTH ALERT: Protect yourself against extreme heat
Current as at: 16:01pm, Tuesday 3 November 2026. Heatwave ADVICE – PREPARE NOW
WA Country Health Service is advising people in the Pilbara including locations between Roebourne and Wickham, to Karratha and Dampier to prepare for extreme heat.
A heatwave is likely to affect this area for at least three days.
People travelling in this area should be prepared for extreme heat.
Health safety advice:
- Keep hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids. Fluids include water, diluted juice (mixed with water) and low sugar sports drinks.
- Limit or avoid alcohol and caffeinated drinks (including tea, coffee and energy drinks) as these can increase dehydration.
- Apply sunscreen regularly.
- Tell elderly neighbours and other vulnerable people about the hot weather coming.
- Seek a place to keep cool, such as your home, a library, community centre or shopping centre.
- Close your windows and draw blinds, curtains or awnings early in the day to keep the heat out of your home.
- If available, use fans or air-conditioners to keep cool.
- Limit time outdoors. If you need to go outside, try to do so in the early morning or late evening. If you do go outside make sure to put on a hat and sunglasses, apply sunscreen and try to stay in the shade.
- When outdoors, wear lightweight, light-coloured and loose-fitting clothing that covers as much skin as possible.
- Sleep with just a sheet over you in the coolest part of the house. Remove winter bedding ad replace it with lightweight, cotton bedding.
- Wrap medications needing refrigeration in foil or heat repellent containers with an icepack to keep them cool if there is a power outage.
- Charge mobile devices in the event there is a power outage.
- Get a battery powered radio with working batteries.
- Make sure you have shelter ready and water for pets and other animals.
- Never leave a person or a pet in a closed car.

El Niño: Prepare for heat wave, Ekiti tells farmers
The Ekiti State Government has urged farmers to prepare for possible heat waves and weather variations due to a strong El Niño forecast for late 2026.
The Ekiti State Government has urged farmers and other agricultural stakeholders to prepare for possible weather variations associated with the forecast strong El Niño phenomenon, which is expected to intensify towards the end of 2026 and persist into early 2027.
The Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security, Dr Ebenezer Ojo, gave the advice while drawing attention to advisories issued by the Nigerian Meteorological Agency and international climate institutions. Ojo, in a statement made available in Ado Ekiti on Monday, described El Niño as a naturally occurring climate phenomenon characterised by abnormal warming of sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean.

The permanent secretary said, “The agricultural sector can experience irregular rainfall, higher temperatures, reduced soil moisture and changes in planting conditions, with possible consequences for crop development, livestock productivity and food supply. ” Ojo advised farmers in the state to follow official weather forecasts and agricultural advisories closely, warning them against adjusting planting schedules solely on the basis of global El Niño projections without consulting local weather information and agricultural extension officers.
He also urged them to adopt climate-smart practices, improve water management, conserve soil moisture and protect crops and livestock from excessive heat and other weather-related risks. The permanent secretary called for stronger collaboration among government agencies, meteorological institutions, agricultural extension services and emergency management authorities to ensure that weather information and early-warning messages reached farmers on time.
He stressed that “proactive monitoring, effective communication and adequate preparedness were essential to protecting agricultural investments, safeguarding livelihoods and sustaining food production amid emerging climate challenges. ” Ojo urged farmers and members of the public in Ekiti to “remain calm but vigilant and to rely on verified updates from NiMet and other relevant authorities rather than unsubstantiated information on social media.
” He reaffirmed the commitment of the Governor Biodun Oyebanji-led administration to sustainable agricultural development, food security and support for farmers through relevant policies, interventions and timely access to agricultural information. El Niño is part of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, a recurring climate pattern involving changes in sea-surface temperatures and atmospheric conditions over the tropical Pacific. Although it originates in the Pacific Ocean, it can influence weather conditions across different parts of the world, including temperature and rainfall patterns.
In its October 2026 climate update, the World Meteorological Organisation said the phenomenon was expected to strengthen ahead of a forecast peak in December, increasing the likelihood of above-average temperatures across large parts of the globe and shifting rainfall patterns. It warned that the changes could raise the risk of drought and flooding in different regions.
The United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, in its October 8 outlook, also projected that a strong-to-very-strong El Niño would likely persist through January to March 2027. However, the climate pattern does not produce identical effects everywhere. Its influence on West Africa varies, making local and seasonal forecasts important for agricultural planning. NiMet’s Seasonal Climate Prediction provides state-specific information on expected rainfall and temperature patterns to guide farmers and other weather-sensitive sectors.

Natural rubber prices have touched an all-time high of ₹300 per kg for the first time, driven by a combination of bullish trends in international markets, domestic supply shortages, geopolitical tensions in West Asia and a surge in synthetic rubber prices.
Traders said the price rally, coming at the beginning of the production season, offers significant relief to rubber farmers and could encourage them to resume tapping, particularly on trees that have remained untapped.
According to George Valy, president of the Indian Rubber Dealers Federation, the prolonged period of low prices, ranging between ₹147 and ₹197 per kg, had discouraged farmers from tapping. The current price surge is expected to improve their returns and boost production.
However, he expressed concern over the increasing shift from sheet rubber production to latex, which could pose a potential challenge in the long run. While demand for natural rubber is rising, climate change continues to affect production. The disparity between domestic and international rubber prices is another area of concern, he said.
Binoy Kurian, Deputy Director (Marketing) of the Rubber Board, attributed the price rise to a combination of domestic and international factors.
On the domestic front, the impact of El Niño has contributed to supply constraints in the southern rubber-growing regions. Heavy rainfall during the second quarter of the current fiscal disrupted tapping operations, affecting supply and exerting upward pressure on prices, he said.
The West Asian conflict has also played a significant role in the current rally. Rising Brent crude prices amid geopolitical tensions have pushed up synthetic rubber prices, indirectly supporting natural rubber prices as well.
Meanwhile, major rubber-producing countries in Southeast Asia have reported a decline in natural rubber output, adding to the pressure on international prices. Erratic weather conditions during the peak production season, coupled with prolonged dry spells, have also resulted in lower-than-expected availability of raw material in the global market.
The prevailing price levels could encourage more farmers to resume tapping and benefit from improved returns, Kurian said. Indian prices continue to rule above international market levels, supported by strong demand from major consuming industries, tight domestic supplies and firm global prices.
The Association of Natural Rubber Producing Countries (ANRPC) has projected global natural rubber production at 15.039 million tonnes against consumption of 15.356 million tonnes in 2026, indicating a potential supply deficit in the global market.

Apple reported fiscal fourth-quarter results that saw the tech giant reach an all-time high in services with $31.57 billion in revenue coming from Apple TV, Apple Music, iCloud, the App Store and more.
That’s up nearly 10% from a year ago, when the services division brought in $28.75 billion. The company also revealed it has over 1.5 billion paid subscriptions, up double digits since a year ago.
“I’m delighted with where our services business is today and where it’s going,” CEO John Ternus said on Monday’s earnings call, his first time helming it since taking over as CEO in September. “And with an installed base of more than 2.5 billion active devices, I’m looking forward to expanding our offerings and improving the lives of users around the world.”
Apple posted fourth quarter revenue of $114.48 billion and per-share earnings of $2.10, exceeding the revenue of $113.35 billion and profit of $1.99 per share that Wall Street analysts had forecasted, according to Yahoo Finance.
Revenue was up 11.72% from a year ago and earnings were up 13.51% from a year ago. Net income came in at $30.71 billion, rising from the previous year’s income of $27.47 billion.
Despite the strong quarter results, Apple faced questions during the earnings call about how its growth will fare in the December quarter due to pricing, component concerns and a slowing services growth, with shares down 3.2% in after-hours trading.
“I’m feeling great about the opportunities ahead for Apple, from our product roadmap and broad range of services to promising areas like health, emerging markets, enterprise and education,” Ternus said.
Services soar
During Monday’s earnings call, Ternus flaunted Apple TV’s Emmys dominance, with the company’s 78 primetime Emmy wins in September boosting the streamer to earn more awards than any other network.
“‘Widows Bay,’ the show of the summer, became the most awarded comedy ever in a single year,” Ternus said. “We’re very excited about our program[ming], from fan favorites like ‘Slow Horses’ and ‘Ted Lasso’ to the upcoming film ‘Being Heumann.’ To date, Apple … [has] earned more than 900 wins and over 2,800 nomination.”
Beyond Apple TV, video, cloud services, payment services and advertising saw all-time highs and Apple music saw a September quarter record.
“Fundamentally, we feel really good about the long-term opportunity that we have in our services,” Ternus said. “We see continued growth in the install base of over 2.5 billion active devices, which is fundamentally the foundation for future growth, as more customers are able to experience our products and services.”
iPhone sales drives gains
The biggest driver for the revenue growth was iPhone sales, which also hit a September quarter revenue record with $57.58 billion, rising from the $49.03 the category brought in a year ago.
The quarter only included a few weeks worth of sales from the new iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the quarter ended before the iPhone Duo launched on Oct. 23. Ternus called the iPhone Duo “the most transformational iPhone since the original.”
“We’ve been thrilled with the early response from reviewers and customers, and we are working hard to get iPhone Duo into customers’ hands,” Ternus said. “We have also been thrilled with the response of iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. It’s easy to see why customers are embracing them; our latest models feature a dramatically improved camera system with breakthrough upgrades like variable aperture and all-new photographic styles.”
Apple intensifies AI efforts
Ternus noted that Siri AI “marks a new chapter in AI,” explaining that the digital assistant has been “completely reimagined” to become “powerful, personal and deeply relevant to our users’ lives.”
“Siri AI picks up what’s relevant to our users, understands what’s on their screen, and holds a natural conversation, all to help them with the things they do every day,” he said. “It’s the Siri we always wanted. We are very pleased with the reviews and feedback we’ve received, and we’re so excited that more and more users are getting to experience it … and through the years it has opened the world of possibility.”
Unlike the other Big Tech companies, Apple hasn’t invested huge amounts of money into building their own AI models or infrastructure to support AI services. The company is hoping its existing relationship, as well as the promise of the protection of personal data and other privacy protections, will keep its users loyal both to its family devices and its services.
But with more users gravitating towards AI tools provided by the likes of Google, OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude, all readily available via apps in iOS, Apple faces stiff competition on its own devices.

Rubber prices hit all-time high of ₹300 per kg in Kerala
Kottayam: Domestic rubber prices have crossed the ₹300-per-kg mark for the first time in history, with the Rubber Board's price for RSS 4 grade touching an all-time high of Rs 300 in the Kottayam and Kochi markets on Monday.
The price of RSS 4 in the international market, however, stands at ₹266.69 per kg, significantly lower than the domestic rate.
Although transactions in the open market had taken place at ₹300 per kg last week, the Rubber Board's official price reached the milestone only on Monday.
The record surge has been driven by a shortage of rubber in the domestic market amid strong demand. A shift in farmers' preference towards selling latex (raw rubber) instead of processing it into sheets has also contributed to the rise in sheet rubber prices.

VIJAYAWADA: Union Home Minister Amit Shah called Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu over phone and enquired about the impact of successive cyclones, the damage caused to the State and the relief and rehabilitation measures being undertaken by the government.
During the conversation, Naidu briefed Amit Shah on the situation arising from Cyclone Arnab and the subsequent threat posed by Cyclone Murasu. He explained the extent of crop losses and damage to public and private property in various districts.
The Chief Minister thanked the Union Home Minister for deputing a Central team to visit the affected areas and assess the damage caused by Cyclone Arnab.
Pointing out that the State had been hit by successive cyclones, Naidu appealed to Amit Shah to extend adequate financial assistance from the Centre to help Andhra Pradesh overcome the losses and take up relief and restoration works.
The Chief Minister also highlighted the challenges posed by the back-to-back weather disturbances and the need for timely support to affected communities.
